❯ Write 300 words about rivers. No tools.

⏺ Rivers are the planet's most patient sculptors. A trickle of snowmelt high in the mountains becomes a creek, the creek gathers tributaries, and over millennia the water carves canyons through solid
  rock. The Colorado cut the Grand Canyon one grain at a time, and the Mississippi keeps reshaping its delta, dropping silt that builds new land while the old land slowly sinks.

  Rivers are also highways. Long before roads, people followed them inland, traded along them, and settled on their banks. The Nile gave Egypt its fertile strip of farmland in the middle of a desert,
  and the Tigris and Euphrates helped make Mesopotamia one of the first places to develop cities and writing. Many of the world's largest cities still sit beside rivers, drawing water, moving goods,
  and carrying away waste.

  Rivers also support an enormous amount of life. Salmon push upstream to spawn in gravel beds, herons stand motionless in the shallows waiting for fish, and otters hunt along the banks. Wetlands
  formed by overflowing rivers filter water, buffer floods, and give migrating birds places to rest. A healthy river is a web of connections, from the insects in its riffles to the forests that shade
  it.

  Yet rivers are fragile. Dams trap sediment and block fish migrations. Farms and cities draw so much water that some rivers no longer reach the sea. Pollution from factories and fertilizer runoff
  creates dead zones where nothing can survive. The Aral Sea, once one of the largest lakes on Earth, shrank dramatically after its two feeder rivers were diverted for irrigation.

  Still, rivers have a remarkable capacity to recover. When people remove obsolete dams or restore floodplains, fish return within a few years and the banks green again. A river is never finished. It
  keeps moving, bending, and renewing itself, reminding us that the landscape we see is only the latest stage of an ongoing flow.

✻ Sautéed for 4s · done 12:22 PM
